notes.title: Parallel conduction and Planckian scattering in FeTeSe
notes.summary: Connect optical parallel-channel fits with Planckian rate conventions and nonlinear resistance, while keeping the pairing mechanism unresolved.

sections.title: What was measured
sections.markdown: Romero and colleagues analyzed complex terahertz conductivity alongside DC resistance in two FeTe1−xSex films. Their model separates a narrow Drude response from a much broader background. Within the measured frequency window, the narrow-channel width is approximately linear in temperature, while the total resistance need not be. The inferred condensate weight is mainly associated with that channel. This is an author-version interpretation, not a unique determination of the pairing interaction.

sections.title: Keep the frequency convention explicit
sections.markdown: For a Drude denominator $\Gamma-i\nu$, both variables use ordinary frequency. The corresponding pole decay rate is $\gamma=2\pi\Gamma$. Thus $\Gamma=\alpha k_BT/h$ and $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$ express the same coefficient after conversion. The inherited reading note mixed these conventions. Its numerical expressions must not be copied unchanged.

sections.title: Why parallel channels matter
sections.markdown:
As a separate local illustration, take fixed $S>0$, $\sigma_0\geq0$, $c>0$, $\Gamma_0\geq0$ and $T>0$:

$$\sigma_{\rm DC}=\sigma_0+\frac{S}{\Gamma_0+cT},\qquad \rho_{\rm DC}=\frac{\Gamma_0+cT}{S+\sigma_0(\Gamma_0+cT)}.$$

Differentiation gives $d\rho_{\rm DC}/dT=cS/[S+\sigma_0(\Gamma_0+cT)]^2$. A linear narrow-channel rate therefore need not give linear total resistivity. When $\sigma_0=0$, this model does recover a linear resistivity. The approximation $\sigma_{\rm DC}=a+b/T$ additionally neglects $\Gamma_0$ and assumes sufficiently constant amplitudes. This algebra is not a fit to the experimental data.

sections.title: What remains unresolved
sections.markdown: The broad contribution is not resolved as an independent complete Drude peak. Its microscopic origin and a unique relaxation coefficient are therefore not established by this fit. The manuscript discusses nematic pairing qualitatively and leaves the mechanism open. Its printed missing-area prefactor requires comparison with the final paper and normalization before precise condensate fractions are imported. No third-party figures or full text are reproduced here.

sections.title: Read the sample series before the headline
sections.markdown:
Bhatt and colleagues compare bilayer La3Ni2O7−δ films on four substrates. The final Figure 1 distinguishes nominal substrate mismatch from measured film strain. Negative values denote compression. The film on SLAO has a broad resistive transition; the other listed films do not establish superconductivity merely because one also has compressive strain.

| Substrate | Nominal strain | Measured strain | Reported transport in this study |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| SLAO | −2.0% | −1.6% | Onset near 42 K; zero resistance around 2 K |
| LAO | −1.2% | −0.9% | Metallic |
| NGO | +0.7% | +0.6% | Metallic |
| STO | +1.9% | +1.8% | Insulating |

These temperature endpoints belong to the SLAO film's ambient-pressure transport report, cited by the structural paper to Ko and colleagues. They are different criteria, not two interchangeable values of a precisely established bulk transition. The growth methods also differ: SLAO uses pulsed-laser deposition, whereas the main comparison films on LAO, NGO and STO use molecular-beam epitaxy. The authors do not definitively exclude sensitivity to synthesis details.

sections.title: Nominal mismatch is not the remaining film strain
sections.markdown:
The methods define nominal mismatch as $\epsilon_{\rm nom}=(a_{\rm sub}-a_{\rm bulk})/a_{\rm bulk}$, using the bulk pseudo-tetragonal reference $a_{\rm bulk}=3.833$ Å. The substrate values are 3.756, 3.787, 3.858 and 3.905 Å for SLAO, LAO, NGO and STO. Direct arithmetic reproduces the rounded nominal percentages in the table; it does not calculate the film's measured relaxation.

In-plane compression and higher octahedral symmetry are common features identified in the superconducting film and pressurized bulk structures. Their out-of-plane responses differ: the film can expand along the stacking direction while a hydrostatically compressed bulk sample contracts. This contrast does not convert epitaxial strain into an equivalent pressure. Nor does it establish that the SLAO film has the largest c-axis among all substrates.

sections.title: What the orbital calculations do and do not establish
sections.markdown:
The study decomposes structural changes into bond-length changes, internal-angle changes and rigid octahedral rotations. Calculations on those separated distortions are hypothetical controls, not independently prepared experimental samples. The reported suppression concerns local $t_{2g}$ admixture in predominantly $e_g$ low-energy bands; it is not a demonstration that the $d_{z^2}$ orbital disappears from the Fermi surface.

The final discussion says the importance of this reduced mixing for superconductivity remains to be established. Rotation effects are considered together with phenomenological Hubbard interactions. The calculations compare band structures, not a reproduced superconducting transition or a uniquely selected pairing mechanism. The metallic LAO film also has similar higher octahedral symmetry, so symmetry alone cannot be treated as a sufficient condition in this series.

sections.title: Keep local structure and superconductivity evidence distinct
sections.markdown:
STEM cannot directly identify which microscopic regions are superconducting. The paper examines defects, mixed structural phases and variable oxygen occupancy that can affect bulk-sensitive transport and diffraction. Its methods coordinate microscopy preparation and measurements within three days of oxygen annealing to mitigate oxygen loss. That protocol is part of the evidence context, not proof of exact oxygen stoichiometry.

The study reports 40 distinct ptychography fields of view for bond analysis. Thousands of bonds within those images are not thousands of independently synthesized superconducting specimens. A low-temperature reversal of oxygen-distortion direction, analogous to that reported in bulk, remains unresolved for the films. Raw imaging reconstructions, transport data, full supplements and DFT convergence have not been reproduced in this editorial check.

sections.title: Use the structural comparison as a constraint
sections.markdown: When comparing a new film, retain its growth and annealing history, composition, reference lattice, measured strain, local structural probe and transition criterion. Compare nominally similar samples before attributing transport changes solely to strain. This note connects the nickelate, strain and transport articles; it does not supply a validated recipe for raising the transition temperature.

notes.summary: Separate sample-specific zero resistance, diamagnetic screening and resistance-contour criteria in Sm/Ca/Eu infinite-layer films; keep exchange compensation, magnetic order and pairing symmetry as distinct questions.

limitations: Author self-review, not independent scientific review or a reproduction of the transport measurements.

Resistance-contour criteria, zero resistance and screening are different observables. None alone settles the magnetic structure or pairing symmetry.

sections.title: Identify the material and the version
sections.markdown:
Yang and colleagues study Sm0.95−xCa0.05EuxNiO2 (SCEₓ), an infinite-layer nickelate film series with fixed nominal Ca substitution. It is not Eu-substituted bilayer La3Ni2O7. The measured Eu valence is mixed and varies with composition, so nominal x is not a direct count of identical Eu²⁺ moments.

This note reads the revised author manuscript dated 25 April 2026. The journal article was published online on 23 April 2026. The publisher abstract supports the broad re-entrance report, but access to that abstract does not establish equivalence of all final and author-version figures. The separate Nd/Eu nickelate study discussed in G3 and G5 concerns another material series; its magnetic interpretation cannot simply be transferred here.

sections.title: Keep each field scale with its sample and criterion
sections.markdown:
The selected author text and Figure 2 distinguish the following observations. Fields are perpendicular to the film plane (H∥c) for these comparisons.

| Sample | Temperature or protocol | Reported observation | Interpretation boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SCE0.34, about 54 unit cells | 2 K transport | Zero resistance returns above about 6.23 T | Recovery field, not a universal upper critical field |
| Same SCE0.34 specimen | Temperature sweeps at fixed field | Mutual-inductance screening at 9 and 12 T; absent at 3 T | Supports the superconducting interpretation; no bulk volume fraction is inferred here |
| SCE0.32 | 3 K transport | Resistance returns to zero near 13.04 T | Not the upper boundary of the high-field phase |
| SCE0.32 | 1.7 K transport | High-field zero resistance persists above about 32 T | Different temperature from the 13.04 T statement |

These temperatures describe measurement conditions, not interchangeable transition temperatures. Figure 3 instead marks open-circle phase boundaries using 0.5Rn, with Rn the high-field normal-state resistance. Those contours must not be relabeled zero-resistance boundaries. No material-Tc record is created from this table.

sections.title: Angular behavior and an unresolved inherited number
sections.markdown:
The angle θ is measured from the film normal. The angular maps use different temperatures: 4.2 K for x=0.33 and 0.36, 1.5 K for x=0.38, and 0.3 K for x=0.40. Their changing angular windows cannot support a universal assertion that in-plane re-entrance is absent. The manuscript also distinguishes intermediate-doping compensation-like behavior from stronger deviations at x=0.40.

The inherited notes attribute persistence to 45 T at 0.3 K to SCE0.36. That exact sample–temperature–field tuple was not verified in the selected v3 pages. Extended Data Figure 9 labels SCE0.36 at 4.2 K and SCE0.40 at 0.3 K; it also has a caption saying “up to 45 T” although its upper panels extend to 60 T. These version and panel details require resolution before the inherited tuple is used as a current verified result. A measurement ceiling would in any case provide a bound, not a measured high-field endpoint.

sections.title: What the magnetic evidence can and cannot establish
sections.markdown:
Nonlinear Hall response after linear-background subtraction and hysteretic magnetoresistance motivate magnetic explanations. They do not by themselves identify uniform ferromagnetism, its volume fraction, or a particular pairing state. The v3 discussion explicitly leaves long-range magnetic order and its structure undetermined.

The authors fit a WHH-based model including orbital and Pauli pair breaking, spin-orbit scattering and an exchange field. Compensation partially describes intermediate compositions; the fitted exchange fields and scattering parameters remain phenomenological. An empirical factor of two in a Brillouin-function argument improves some fits but is not universal and does not adequately describe x=0.40. Neither this adjustment nor analogy with other re-entrant systems proves spin-triplet pairing.

sections.title: Use the result across the Wiki
sections.markdown:
D5 supplies the material-family context; D15 separates substitution, scattering and magnetism; G3 and G5 distinguish re-entrance from a demonstrated compensation mechanism. For H7 and H9, superconducting recovery fields must not become Hall-sign-reversal or anomalous-Hall threshold fields. This note reports no extracted ordinary Hall coefficient.

A stronger scientific assessment still needs version-resolved final figures, criterion and noise-floor checks, sample calibration and local magnetic probes. The present review neither fits the deposited source-data files nor certifies an intrinsic bulk phase or unique microscopic mechanism.

notes.title: Pressure-quenched Hg1223: onset, magnetic response and stability
notes.summary: Follow the sample histories behind the reported 151 K resistive onset. Magnetic-volume estimates, storage tests and an unreproduced 172 K anomaly belong to distinct specimens and protocols.

review.scope: Selected arXiv:2603.12437v1 text, methods and figures, including supplementary figures contained in that author PDF. Publication metadata checked separately; complete final-version and final-supplement equivalence remain open.
limitations: Author self-review; no independent replication, raw-data refitting or material certification.
The 151 K value is an onset criterion for S4. Retrieved S2 magnetization and S3 storage tests cannot be transferred to that specimen.
This note does not assign a superconducting transition to the unreproduced 172 K anomaly or establish room-temperature storage durability.

sections.title: Preparation pressure is not measurement pressure
sections.markdown:
Deng and colleagues compress HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ, cool it, and release pressure at a chosen quench temperature. Their quoted post-quench transitions are measured at ambient pressure, after a high-pressure preparation history. The transition criterion is the rapid change of dR/dT used to identify resistive onset; it is not a zero-resistance temperature.

The selected author manuscript defines a transition width as onset minus the temperature at 50% of the onset resistance. Reported widths therefore cannot silently become onset-to-zero widths. Multiple experiments within the paper are not independent laboratory replication.

sections.title: Read the experiments as separate sample histories
sections.markdown:
The author text and Figure 2 report the following ambient-pressure onsets after quenching. The pressure and temperature columns describe preparation.

| Experiment / sample | Quench pressure | Quench temperature | Retained resistive onset |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 1 / S1 | 26.0 GPa | 77 K | 139 K on repeated warming |
| 2 / S1 | 28.4 GPa | 4.2 K | 147 K warming and cooling |
| 3 / S2 | 10.1 GPa | 4.2 K | 147 K warming and cooling |
| 4 / S3 | 10.9 GPa | 4.2 K | 149 K warming; 148 K cooling |
| 5 / S4 | 18.9 GPa | 4.2 K | 151 K warming; 150 K cooling |

S1 is used twice; the rows are not five independent specimens. The five specimens S1–S5 came from three parent crystals, with S1, S2 and S4 cut from the same parent crystal. Different quench pressure, thermal history and specimen identity prevent interpreting this table as a one-variable controlled comparison. The highest onset in these rows is not evidence for a 151 K zero-resistance threshold.

sections.title: The magnetic estimate belongs to retrieved S2
sections.markdown:
After its 10.1 GPa / 4.2 K preparation and retrieval from the pressure cell, S2 shows a magnetic transition near 140 K in 10 Oe. The approximately 78% estimate uses its magnetic moment at 70 K and an approximate disk geometry. It is not a 78% superconducting-volume measurement on S4 at 151 K.

The methods use $f\simeq\pi(|M|/H)/r^3$ in their stated cgs convention, with $|M|/H=1.9\times10^{-8}$ emu/Oe and $r=42.5\times10^{-4}$ cm. Direct substitution gives $f\simeq0.778$, matching the reported rounded estimate. This arithmetic check does not validate the sample geometry, background subtraction or demagnetization approximation. The cubic radius dependence makes geometry consequential.

Figure S6 multiplies the post-quench curve by ten for display and compares it with the pristine parent crystal. Comparing the plotted amplitudes as if they were unscaled, identical-volume specimens would mislead.

sections.title: Cold retention and the unreproduced anomaly
sections.markdown:
The temporal test uses S3 after a 10.9 GPa / 4.2 K quench. Storage at 77 K for up to three days, interrupted by measurements reaching 160–170 K, retains the elevated onset with a small decrease. A separate S2 thermal cycle reaching 293 K lowers its onset from about 147 K to 143 K. These observations do not establish room-temperature shelf life for the highest-onset S4 specimen.

S5, quenched from 29.7 GPa at 4.2 K, shows a broad warming anomaly extending to about 172 K. The author text describes warming to 193 K and subsequent cooling from 180 K; the high-temperature feature disappears on cooling and was not reproduced. Its nature remains unresolved. This note keeps it as an unassigned anomaly, not an accepted superconducting transition or a searchable material-Tc record.

sections.title: Separate structural observations from a proposed mechanism
sections.markdown:
Selected diffraction measurements retain the average tetragonal assignment through the measured pressure range, up to about 15 GPa, and after quenching. The (200) peak width increases from about 0.12° before compression to 0.20° after quenching. Figure 3 also marks unidentified peaks and distinguishes apparatus-related peaks. These observations cannot exclude every minority phase or prove a unique defect-stabilization mechanism.

Calculations predict a pressure-driven Lifshitz change near 12.5 GPa, involving apical-oxygen-derived states. A calculated pocket and density-of-states increase is not direct observation that those states survive pressure release, nor proof that they cause the retained onset. The proposed metastability barrier and roles of strain, defects and oxygen require further tests. No universal transfer of this protocol to another material is established here.

sections.title: Use the result without combining incompatible evidence
sections.markdown: Read E10 for metastability and kinetic assumptions, D3 for cuprate context, and A1/A2 for transport and magnetic criteria. N1 distinguishes a high but finite onset from a room-temperature claim. An assessment should keep preparation history, measurement pressure, criterion, specimen, thermal cycle and source version together. The original reading note is retained as provenance; this synthesis replaces its overgeneralized bulk, storage and mechanism claims.

sections.title: Read layer order and criterion together
sections.markdown:
Gozar’s author version defines I as La2CuO4, M as La1.55Sr0.45CuO4, and S as oxygen-doped La2CuO4+δ. The first letter denotes the layer nearest the substrate. Its typical resistive midpoints are approximately 15 K for I–M and 30 K for M–I; ozone-treated M–S structures reach about 50 K. These are distinct preparations.

Thickness and screening analyses constrain a roughly one-to-two-unit-cell interfacial region within their models. Microscopy bounds cation intermixing around one unit cell; it does not prove atomically perfect chemistry. The authors retain several possible enhancement mechanisms.

sections.title: What the single-plane abstract supports
sections.markdown:
Logvenov and colleagues describe molecular-beam-grown metal/insulator bilayers, with each block three unit cells thick. Layer-selective Zn substitution acts as a suppressing marker; their abstract attributes the interface superconductivity to one CuO2 plane.

This is a localization inference in a heterostructure, not an isolated free-standing plane. The full methods, Zn profile and calibration have not been reviewed here. No new composition or transition-temperature record is assigned from the abstract. The publisher’s deposited editorial summary and the original abstract are also kept distinct.

sections.title: Compare evidence without combining experiments
sections.markdown:
An editorial comparison should retain the sample stack, treatment, observable and criterion for each result. A thickness-dependent transition, a screening model and a layer-selective perturbation answer related but different questions. A model-dependent length estimate should not be silently converted to a direct spatial image. Nor does localization alone determine the highest achievable transition temperature or select a unique pairing mechanism.

Pressure-quenched Hg1223 is a separate preparation problem. The [Hg1223 research note](/scwiki/library/deng-hg1223-pressure-quench) preserves its specimen histories; those results should not be entered as cuprate-interface measurements.

sections.markdown:

Studies 3 and 5 have separate [magnetic-excitation](/scwiki/library/dean-lsco-magnetic-excitations) and [THz conductivity](/scwiki/library/bilbro-thz-fluctuation-window) notes. Superfluid-density scaling, ultrafast crystallography, proximity effects, antiferromagnetism, the superconductor–insulator transition and the plasmon study remain separate review tasks.

The repaired parsed-file directory contains curated source notes, not original-paper transcriptions. A bibliography is not a checked primary passage.

sections.title: A conductivity window, not a universal pairing cutoff
sections.markdown: Bilbro and colleagues studied eight LSCO films, $x=0.09$–$0.25$. Their THz conductivity criterion places the fluctuation onset 5–16 K above $T_c$. They determine onset from the curvature of $\omega\sigma_2$ at 0.8 THz. This is a probe-dependent transport result, not exclusion of all higher-temperature pairing. Figure 3 assigns $T_c=23.5$ K to $x=0.25$.

sections.title: Keep the rate convention and scale uncertainty
sections.markdown: The angular-rate form is $\Omega=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$; the plotted cyclic frequency is $\Omega/(2\pi)=\alpha k_BT/h$. Methods set $\alpha=0.4$ to the mean after a loss-peak normalization gives a roughly 40% spread. It is not a precision universal constant. The authors cannot distinguish normal-state masking from intrinsically linear-in-temperature fluctuations.

sections.title: Use the measured observable in comparisons
sections.markdown:
An editorial comparison should record the sample, probe frequency, onset criterion, background treatment and rate definition before comparing a transport result with a magnetic signal. A common temperature dependence alone does not identify a common mechanism.

Keep these film measurements separate from [interface localization](/scwiki/library/cuprate-interface-layer-order). This note is not a new transition-temperature record in the material-condition catalogue.

sections.title: Coverage and source version
sections.markdown:
This note covers study 5 of the inherited ten-study series. Studies 2 and 9 have [separate interface coverage](/scwiki/library/cuprate-interface-layer-order); study 3 has a [magnetic-excitation note](/scwiki/library/dean-lsco-magnetic-excitations), and the other six remain pending. The provenance records partial coverage of both source notes.

Use the archive submission date for this source version. Its printed typesetting date is not the journal publication date. The arXiv distribution license is not a general permission to reproduce the paper.

notes.title: LSCO magnetic excitations: persistence within a measured window
notes.summary: Follow the momentum range, linewidth and intensity corrections before drawing a conclusion about superconducting pairing.

review.scope: Selected journal text, Figure 3 and supplementary fitting, normalization and spectral-weight sections. The sample-thickness discrepancy remains unresolved.
limitations: Author self-review; no independent scientific acceptance or raw-data refitting.
The journal main text and supplementary Table I disagree on two sample thicknesses. No silent reconciliation is applied.
Study 3 adds limited coverage to studies 2, 5 and 9; six inherited series studies remain pending.

sections.title: Persistence has a momentum window
sections.markdown: Dean and colleagues find broadened magnetic excitations in LSCO up to $x=0.40$. Their reported fitted window is $\mathbf Q=(0.18\text{–}0.40,0)$ in reciprocal lattice units. It complements neutron measurements near $(0.5,0.5)$. Similar dispersion and comparable integrated intensity in this window do not establish conservation across the whole Brillouin zone.

sections.title: Widths and intensities need their corrections
sections.markdown: The resolution is 130 meV **HWHM**, not FWHM. Fits include a thermal factor and resolution convolution. Unresolved phonon/multispin scattering contributes an estimated 15% overestimate to width and intensity. Supplementary intensity corrections include a changed incident flux and a 0.78 factor for the nominally thicker films; instrumental instability enters the uncertainty.

sections.title: An unresolved sample-thickness discrepancy
sections.markdown: The main-text grouping assigns approximately 53 nm to $x=0.16$ and 99 nm to $x=0.26$. Supplementary Table I instead lists $97\pm3$ nm and $52\pm3$ nm, respectively. The normalization discussion follows the former grouping. These records are not reconciled here; the corrected intensities have not been independently reproduced.

sections.title: What the spectral-fraction estimate assumes
sections.markdown: The quoted 27% spectral fraction comes from an undoped spin-wave calculation. Extending its persistence with doping assumes comparable scaling along an unmeasured diagonal direction.

sections.title: Use spectral evidence to constrain a pairing model
sections.markdown: Editorially, persistence of an excitation is one constraint on a pairing theory. It cannot by itself select a unique interaction or explain the transition temperature. Compare the relevant momentum, energy and sample conditions, rather than treating an integrated signal as a complete pairing kernel.

sections.title: Coverage within the inherited research series
sections.markdown:
This note covers study 3. [Interface localization](/scwiki/library/cuprate-interface-layer-order) covers studies 2 and 9; [THz conductivity](/scwiki/library/bilbro-thz-fluctuation-window) covers study 5. Six studies and additional cross-topic comparisons remain pending.

Each source keeps its own uncertainty and access limits. The source-note merge remains partial; a linked paper does not mean every claim has been independently reviewed.
